input.content:
Every "quick fix" I've shipped without a checklist has come back to bite me within a sprint.

Code review is not a vibe check. It's a repeatable process, and a shared checklist is what turns "looks good to me" into something you can actually trust. I've been using one on my team for the last six months, and the change in review quality has been hard to ignore.

Three takeaways from making the switch:

1. Reviews get faster, not slower. A checklist removes the "what should I even look for?" tax and lets reviewers focus on the parts that need real judgment.

2. Feedback stops being personal. When the standard lives in a shared document, comments read as "the checklist flagged this," not "I don't like your code."

3. Juniors ramp up in weeks, not months. The checklist doubles as onboarding — a written map of what "good" looks like in your codebase.

What's the one item you'd never remove from your review checklist?
